mcq.q: Veraison is the stage when berries
choices: B Soften and change colour as sugar rises
mcq.answer: B Soften and change colour as sugar rises
mcq.why: Veraison marks the start of ripening: colour, sugar up, acid down.

mcq.q: Hail is a serious vineyard hazard because it
choices: A Only cools the fruit with no other effect
B Can strip leaves and split berries, opening the way to rot
C Improves noble rot every year
D Is easily blocked by a cover crop
mcq.answer: B Can strip leaves and split berries, opening the way to rot
mcq.why: Physical damage cuts yield and invites grey rot.

mcq.q: A dense canopy that shades the fruit zone tends to produce
choices: A Thicker skins and more colour
B Unripe flavours, higher disease pressure and thinner skins
D No change if the variety is white
mcq.answer: B Unripe flavours, higher disease pressure and thinner skins
mcq.why: Shade delays ripeness and keeps humidity around the bunches.

mcq.q: Head-trained bush vines (gobelet) are often used in
choices: A Cool, wet sites that need high trellises for air
B Hot, dry, windy sites where a low head shades the fruit
mcq.answer: B Hot, dry, windy sites where a low head shades the fruit
mcq.why: Low, free-standing heads suit Mediterranean drought and wind.

mcq.q: The saignée method of rosé also
choices: A Dilutes the remaining red wine
B Concentrates the remaining red must by bleeding off juice
C Stops MLF in the rosé
mcq.answer: B Concentrates the remaining red must by bleeding off juice
mcq.why: Saignée is a by-product of red winemaking; the pink juice is fermented as rosé.

mcq.q: New American oak, compared with new French oak, typically gives
choices: A Finer tannin and subtler spice only
B More coconut and vanilla aroma
mcq.answer: B More coconut and vanilla aroma
mcq.why: American oak is richer in coconut/vanillin; French oak is usually tighter and spicier.

mcq.q: A cultured yeast is chosen over ambient yeast when the producer wants
choices: A Maximum vintage variation and risk of stuck ferment
B A reliable, complete ferment and a predictable profile
C Flor to form in every tank
D No need for temperature control
mcq.answer: B A reliable, complete ferment and a predictable profile
mcq.why: Selected strains start cleanly and finish dry; wild yeasts are less predictable.

mcq.q: Whole-bunch pressing for white or sparkling base wines is used to
choices: A Maximise phenolics from stalks and seeds
B Give a gentle, pale, low-solids juice
C Extract as much red colour as possible
mcq.answer: B Give a gentle, pale, low-solids juice
mcq.why: Intact bunches act as a filter; Champagne and quality whites often start this way.

mcq.q: Margaux, compared with Saint-Estèphe, is often described as
choices: A The most tannic, clay-heavy northern Médoc commune
B A more fragrant, finer-boned southern Médoc commune
D A Right Bank limestone plateau
mcq.answer: B A more fragrant, finer-boned southern Médoc commune
mcq.why: Margaux’s gravels give perfume; Saint-Estèphe is cooler, more clay, firmer.

mcq.q: Cadillac, Loupiac and Sainte-Croix-du-Mont make
choices: B Sweet white wines in the orbit of Sauternes, usually simpler and cheaper
mcq.answer: B Sweet white wines in the orbit of Sauternes, usually simpler and cheaper
mcq.why: They sit across the Garonne from Sauternes; same grapes, less prestige.

mcq.q: Gevrey-Chambertin and Vosne-Romanée are
choices: A Côte de Beaune Chardonnay villages
B Côte de Nuits Pinot Noir villages with Grand Crus
mcq.answer: B Côte de Nuits Pinot Noir villages with Grand Crus
mcq.why: Two of the Côte de Nuits’ most famous red villages.

mcq.q: Montagny and Rully blanc are
choices: A Chardonnay wines of the Côte Chalonnaise
mcq.answer: A Chardonnay wines of the Côte Chalonnaise
mcq.why: Chalonnaise whites: more modest than Beaune, same grape.

mcq.q: Saumur-Champigny is a red appellation for
choices: B Cabernet Franc on tuffeau around Saumur
mcq.answer: B Cabernet Franc on tuffeau around Saumur
mcq.why: Anjou-Saumur’s best-known red; floral, leafy, often unoaked or lightly oaked.

mcq.q: Quarts de Chaume is
choices: A A dry Savennières lieu-dit with no sweet wine
B A small, sweet Chenin Blanc AOC in the Layon, with grand cru status
mcq.answer: B A small, sweet Chenin Blanc AOC in the Layon, with grand cru status
mcq.why: One of the Loire’s sweet grand cru sites; noble rot Chenin.

mcq.q: Crozes-Hermitage, compared with Hermitage, is
choices: B A larger, often flatter appellation, more variable in quality
mcq.answer: B A larger, often flatter appellation, more variable in quality
mcq.why: Mostly plateau and plain; some hillside fruit approaches Hermitage.

mcq.q: Saint-Joseph reds are
choices: B Syrah from the Northern Rhône’s right bank, lighter than Hermitage on average
mcq.answer: B Syrah from the Northern Rhône’s right bank, lighter than Hermitage on average
mcq.why: A long, thin AOC; quality depends on slope versus river-flat fruit.

mcq.q: Picpoul de Pinet is a
choices: A Full oaked red from Minervois
B Dry, high-acid white from the Languedoc lagoon coast
mcq.answer: B Dry, high-acid white from the Languedoc lagoon coast
mcq.why: Picpoul (Piquepoul) with seafood; a named Languedoc white.

mcq.q: Alsace Riesling Grand Cru is typically
choices: A Low acid and always lusciously sweet
B Dry or off-dry, high acid, and labelled with the vineyard
C A Prädikat Kabinett by German rules
mcq.answer: B Dry or off-dry, high acid, and labelled with the vineyard
mcq.why: Alsace Riesling is usually dry in intent at Grand Cru; VT/SGN are labelled as such.

mcq.q: Dolcetto, compared with Nebbiolo, is typically
choices: A Paler, higher in tannin and longer-lived
B Deeper in colour, lower in acid, and meant for earlier drinking
C Always a sweet dessert wine despite the name
mcq.answer: B Deeper in colour, lower in acid, and meant for earlier drinking
mcq.why: The name is misleading: dry, fruity, everyday Piedmont red.

mcq.q: Carmignano and Bolgheri are Tuscan appellations associated with
choices: B Sangiovese and/or Bordeaux varieties (the Super Tuscan story)
mcq.answer: B Sangiovese and/or Bordeaux varieties (the Super Tuscan story)
mcq.why: Carmignano long allowed Cabernet; Bolgheri is the coastal home of many Super Tuscans.

mcq.q: Recioto della Valpolicella is
choices: B The sweet wine from dried Valpolicella grapes, fermentation stopped with sugar left
mcq.answer: B The sweet wine from dried Valpolicella grapes, fermentation stopped with sugar left
mcq.why: Recioto is the historic sweet wine; Amarone is its dry sibling.

mcq.q: Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo are
choices: B Campanian dry whites with more body and flavour than generic Pinot Grigio
mcq.answer: B Campanian dry whites with more body and flavour than generic Pinot Grigio
mcq.why: Southern Italian whites that can age; volcanic/hilly Irpinia.

mcq.q: Toro, on the Duero, is known for
choices: B Ripe, high-alcohol Tinta de Toro (Tempranillo) reds
mcq.answer: B Ripe, high-alcohol Tinta de Toro (Tempranillo) reds
mcq.why: Warmer and often more powerful than Ribera; same grape family.

mcq.q: Bierzo’s leading red grape is
mcq.answer: A Mencía
mcq.why: Mencía: Atlantic-continental fringe, red fruit and a floral note.

mcq.q: White Rioja traditionally relied on
choices: B Viura (Macabeo), sometimes with long oak ageing
mcq.answer: B Viura (Macabeo), sometimes with long oak ageing
mcq.why: Old-school white Rioja can be nutty and long-oaked; modern styles are fresher.

mcq.q: Pfalz Riesling, compared with Mosel, is often
choices: A Even lighter and more spritzy
B Drier, riper and a little fuller, from a warmer, drier region
mcq.answer: B Drier, riper and a little fuller, from a warmer, drier region
mcq.why: Pfalz is Germany’s sunnier south-west; much quality Riesling is trocken.

mcq.q: Naoussa in northern Greece is associated with
choices: B Xinomavro, a high-acid, tannic red sometimes likened to Nebbiolo
mcq.answer: B Xinomavro, a high-acid, tannic red sometimes likened to Nebbiolo
mcq.why: Xinomavro from Macedonia: tomato, olive, long-lived when well made.

mcq.q: Douro unfortified whites are often based on
choices: B Local grapes such as Viosinho, Rabigato and Gouveio
mcq.answer: B Local grapes such as Viosinho, Rabigato and Gouveio
mcq.why: The same white varieties that can go into white Port, fermented dry.

mcq.q: Baga in Bairrada needs
choices: A A short carbonic ferment only, never oak
B Ripe seeds and careful extraction because tannin and acid are naturally high
C Chaptalisation every year by law
mcq.answer: B Ripe seeds and careful extraction because tannin and acid are naturally high
mcq.why: Late, thick-skinned Baga is harsh if picked or extracted badly.

mcq.q: Finger Lakes Riesling benefits from
choices: A Desert heat like Mendoza’s lowest vineyards
B Lakes that moderate autumn frost in a cool continental climate
mcq.answer: B Lakes that moderate autumn frost in a cool continental climate
mcq.why: New York’s deep lakes store heat; Riesling is the stand-out variety.

mcq.q: Colchagua and Maipo in Chile are best known for
choices: A The country’s coolest Sauvignon Blanc
B Ripe Cabernet Sauvignon and other reds in a warm, sheltered setting
mcq.answer: B Ripe Cabernet Sauvignon and other reds in a warm, sheltered setting
mcq.why: Central Valley warmth; Maipo especially for Cabernet; Colchagua also Carmenère.

mcq.q: Clare and Eden Valley are Australian sources of
choices: B Riesling that is usually dry, high-acid and long-lived in bottle
mcq.answer: B Riesling that is usually dry, high-acid and long-lived in bottle
mcq.why: South Australia’s Riesling belt; lime, toast with age, screwcap culture.

mcq.q: Martinborough (Wairarapa) is known for
choices: B Pinot Noir in a cool, windy corner of the North Island
mcq.answer: B Pinot Noir in a cool, windy corner of the North Island
mcq.why: Low-yielding, structured Pinot; a New Zealand benchmark beside Central Otago.

mcq.q: A wine labelled Vin de France may
choices: B State variety and vintage, but not a smaller GI, and has few origin rules
D Only be sold in France
mcq.answer: B State variety and vintage, but not a smaller GI, and has few origin rules
mcq.why: The bottom EU tier: blending freedom across France.

mcq.q: An Austrian DAC wine is
choices: B A regional PDO that defines typical grapes and style for that area
C A PGI with no grape rules
mcq.answer: B A regional PDO that defines typical grapes and style for that area
mcq.why: Districtus Austriae Controllatus: e.g. Kamptal DAC Riesling or Grüner.

mcq.q: Organic on a wine label refers first to
choices: A Zero sulphur in the cellar always
B Grape growing without synthetic herbicides, pesticides or mineral fertilisers
C The use of only new oak
mcq.answer: B Grape growing without synthetic herbicides, pesticides or mineral fertilisers
mcq.why: Organic is a vineyard (and, if ‘organic wine’, a cellar) certification; SO2 is usually still allowed in limits.

mcq.q: The Montagne de Reims is planted chiefly with
choices: B Pinot Noir, giving body to many blends
mcq.answer: B Pinot Noir, giving body to many blends
mcq.why: North-facing and other aspects still ripen Pinot on the mountain’s chalk.

mcq.q: Transfer method sparkling wine has its second fermentation in
choices: A Tank only, with no lees
B Bottle, then is emptied under pressure into tank for clarification before rebottling
mcq.answer: B Bottle, then is emptied under pressure into tank for clarification before rebottling
mcq.why: Used to avoid riddling while keeping bottle-ferment character; not the same as Charmat.

mcq.q: Blanquette de Limoux, historically, is based on
choices: B Mauzac, with a traditional-method sparkle
mcq.answer: B Mauzac, with a traditional-method sparkle
mcq.why: Languedoc’s old sparkling AOC; Crémant de Limoux leans more on Chardonnay and Chenin.

mcq.q: Cap Classique on a South African label means
mcq.answer: B Traditional-method sparkling wine
mcq.why: The local name for bottle-fermented sparkling; Chardonnay and Pinot are common.

mcq.q: A Blanc de Noirs Champagne is made from
choices: B Black grapes (Pinot Noir and/or Meunier) as a white sparkling wine
C A blend that must include 50% still red wine
mcq.answer: B Black grapes (Pinot Noir and/or Meunier) as a white sparkling wine
mcq.why: Gentle press keeps the juice white; the style is usually fuller than a Blanc de Blancs.

mcq.q: Pale Cream Sherry is typically
choices: B A biologically aged wine that has been sweetened
mcq.answer: B A biologically aged wine that has been sweetened
mcq.why: Sweetened Fino-style wine; Cream is usually a sweetened Oloroso.

mcq.q: Ruby Port is aged
choices: A For decades in bottle before release
B A short time in wood or tank to keep a deep colour and primary fruit
mcq.answer: B A short time in wood or tank to keep a deep colour and primary fruit
mcq.why: Inexpensive, fruity, not for long cellaring; Reserve Ruby is a step up.

mcq.q: Sercial Madeira is the style that is
mcq.answer: B The driest, highest-acid Madeira
mcq.why: Sercial → Verdelho → Bual → Malmsey runs dry to sweet.

mcq.q: Muscat de Rivesaltes is
choices: B A Roussillon VDN that may be made from Muscat grapes
mcq.answer: B A Roussillon VDN that may be made from Muscat grapes
mcq.why: Large VDN AOC; also made as Grenache-based Rivesaltes in other colours/styles.

mcq.q: The solera system in Jerez is designed to
choices: A Keep each vintage separate in bottle
B Blend many ages so style is consistent and young wine feeds the flor
mcq.answer: B Blend many ages so style is consistent and young wine feeds the flor
mcq.why: Criaderas refresh the solera; biological wines need nutrients for flor.

mcq.q: Brettanomyces as a fault typically smells of
choices: A Lime zest and white flowers
B Bandage, sweat or stable, with flattened fruit
mcq.answer: B Bandage, sweat or stable, with flattened fruit
mcq.why: A little can be ‘complex’; when it dominates, the wine is faulty.

mcq.q: Vintage Port with bottle sediment should be
choices: A Served straight from a dusty bin without standing up
B Stood up, then decanted off the crust
C Shaken to mix the crust in
D Served ice-cold in a flute
mcq.answer: B Stood up, then decanted off the crust
mcq.why: Decant for sediment (and some air); a 20-year tawny has none.

mcq.q: Salty food generally makes a wine taste
choices: A More bitter and less fruity
B Fuller and less acidic, and can soften tannin
C Much sweeter than a dessert
mcq.answer: B Fuller and less acidic, and can soften tannin
mcq.why: Salt is one of the more wine-friendly tastes if the wine has enough fruit and acid.

mcq.q: Ideal long-term cellar conditions are closest to
choices: A 20–25 °C with daily swings, bright light
B About 10–15 °C, dark, humid enough, little vibration
D A garage that heats up in summer
mcq.answer: B About 10–15 °C, dark, humid enough, little vibration
mcq.why: Steady cool temperature and darkness matter more than an exact number.

parts.prompt: Describe Alsace’s climate and the vineyard factors that allow both dry and late-harvest wines.
points: Dry, sunny, sheltered by the Vosges rain shadow; continental, cold winters.
Long autumns allow late harvest and, in some years, noble rot (SGN).
Steep, varied geology (granite, limestone, schist, sandstone, volcanic).
Grand Cru sites are named hillsides with defined varieties.
Foehn / dryness reduces disease vs the Rhine plain.
Vendanges Tardives needs high must weight; SGN needs botrytis selection.

parts.prompt: For Riesling, Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris, state typical aroma, sweetness and body in Alsace.
points: Riesling: high acid, citrus/stone/petrol with age, usually dry at GC, most ‘transparent’ to site.
Gewurztraminer: low-medium acid, full body, lychee/rose/spice, often off-dry even when not VT.
Pinot Gris: medium acid, full, bakers’ spice and stone fruit, often some RS.
Muscat (if mentioned) is grapey and usually dry as an aperitif wine.
Pinot Blanc / Sylvaner as lighter supporting varieties can score.
Pinot Noir is the only black grape of note.

parts.prompt: Outline typical winery choices for a dry Grand Cru Riesling versus a Vendange Tardive Gewurztraminer.
points: Riesling: protective, cool ferment, stainless or old wood, ferment dry, no new oak, no MLF usually, early or short élevage.
VT Gewurz: later pick, more sugar, ferment may stop with RS, richer texture, still little new oak.
Both: variety-labelled, often single site.
Avoid carbonic or heavy toast.
SGN would be even sweeter, botrytis-selected.
State the style contrast clearly.

parts.prompt: Explain how granite soils, Gamay and carbonic or semi-carbonic maceration shape Beaujolais Nouveau and a cru such as Morgon.
points: Gamay: thin skin, high acid, low-medium tannin, red fruit.
Granite and schist in the crus (north); clay/limestone more in the south (Bas Beaujolais).
Carbonic / semi-carbonic: whole bunches, intracellular ferment, low tannin, banana/kirsch, early drink.
Nouveau: shortest maceration, released in November, simple and grapey.
Crus (Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent, Fleurie, etc.): often more crushed fruit, longer cuvaison, some oak, can age (Morgon ‘roches pourries’).
Name at least two crus accurately.

parts.prompt: Contrast a village Mâcon-Villages Chardonnay with a Pouilly-Fuissé.
points: Both Chardonnay in a warmer, more Mediterranean-tinged south Burgundy.
Mâcon-Villages: larger area, often tank, early release, apple/citrus, modest price.
Pouilly-Fuissé (and St-Véran, Viré-Clessé): better limestone slopes, more body, sometimes oak, higher quality ceiling.
Premier Cru now exists in Pouilly-Fuissé (if mentioned, can score).
Both riper than Chablis.
Do not confuse Pouilly-Fuissé with Pouilly-Fumé.

parts.prompt: What vineyard or winery choice would raise quality in a high-volume Beaujolais, and what is a risk of overusing carbonic maceration?
points: Lower yield, older vines, cru fruit, some destemmed conventional ferment, oak or lees for texture.
Hand harvest is required for true whole-bunch carbonic.
Risk: all wines taste of banana/process, lack site, do not age, sameness.
Semi-carbonic as a middle path.
Sorting and avoiding grey rot in a wet year.
Award for canopy/airflow on Gamay’s tight bunches.

parts.prompt: Why do most Champagne houses blend across villages, varieties and reserve wines for a non-vintage Brut?
points: Cool climate and vintage variation: one year may lack ripeness or be hit by frost/rain.
House style must be recognisable every year.
Varieties contribute different structure (PN body, Meunier fruit, Chardonnay line).
Villages differ (Côte des Blancs vs Montagne vs Marne vs Bar).
Reserve wines add weight, age notes and consistency.
Blending is done after the first ferment on the vins clairs.
Volume for a global brand.

parts.prompt: How is a rosé Champagne typically made, and how does it differ from most still French rosé?
points: Two legal routes: blend still red with still white before tirage (unusual in still AOC France) or short maceration / saignée.
Still French AOC rosé almost never allows blending red and white (except Champagne).
Red wine for blend often from Pinot Noir (e.g. Bouzy).
Then the same traditional method as white Champagne.
Style: red-fruit note, sometimes more body; dosage usually Brut.
Award for mentioning rosé de saignée as a minority, more structured style.

parts.prompt: Outline dosage levels from Brut Nature to Demi-sec and suggest who each might be served to.
points: Brut Nature / Zéro: 0–3 g/L, no sugar added — lean, for aperitif lovers of high acid.
Extra Brut 0–6; Brut 0–12 — the standard.
Extra Dry 12–17; Sec 17–32 — slightly sweet, with lightly sweet canapés.
Demi-sec 32–50 — cakes, fruit, not bone-dry food.
Doux above 50 is rare.
Always serve well chilled.

parts.prompt: Describe how a vin doux naturel such as Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise is made.
points: Aromatic Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, ripe in a warm southern climate.
Crush/press, start ferment, add grape spirit (mutage) while sugar remains.
Aim is to keep grapey, floral primary fruit; often short, protective ageing in tank.
Bottled young; not a long oxidative solera like Rutherglen or PX.
Strength typically mid-teens % abv plus residual sugar.
Contrast with dry Alsace Muscat if mentioned.

parts.prompt: Contrast that wine with a Rutherglen Muscat in climate, ageing and flavour.
points: Rutherglen: very hot north-east Victoria; brown Muscat (Muscat à Petits Grains Rouge).
Fortified and aged oxidatively in old casks, often a solera-like stack; evaporation concentrates.
Classifications: Rutherglen / Classic / Grand / Rare by age and richness.
Flavours: raisin, stewed fruit, tea, toffee, spice; deep brown; luscious.
Beaumes: pale-gold, grape/orange blossom/rose, youthful.
Both sweet; Rutherglen is far more developed and dense.

parts.prompt: Give service temperatures and one pairing for each wine.
points: Beaumes: well chilled, small glass, aperitif or with fruit / light tarts / blue cheese.
Rutherglen: slightly cool, not ice-cold (aromas set); Christmas pudding, dark chocolate, strong blue.
Opened Beaumes keeps a few days in the fridge; Rutherglen keeps much longer.
Match sweetness to the dish.
Do not serve either at tannic-red temperature.
